title: Reverse Vowels of a String
description:
# Reverse Vowels of a String

Given a string `s`, reverse only the vowels in the string and return the resulting string.

The vowels are `a`, `e`, `i`, `o`, and `u`. They can appear in lowercase or uppercase, and every vowel occurrence participates in the reversal. All non-vowel characters must stay at their original indices. The letter `y` is not considered a vowel for this problem.

## Example 1:

**Input:** s = "hello"
**Output:** "holle"
**Explanation:** The vowels are `e` and `o`; reversing them gives `o` and `e`.

## Example 2:

**Input:** s = "leetcode"
**Output:** "leotcede"

## Constraints:

*   `1 <= s.length <= 3 * 10^5`
*   `s` consists of printable ASCII characters.

solutions.name: Two-Pointer Membership Scan
solutions.description:
## Approach

Convert the string to a character array. Move a left pointer forward until it reaches a vowel, move a right pointer backward until it reaches a vowel, then swap those two vowels and continue inward.

## Key Insight

Only vowel positions are allowed to change. Two pointers find the next pair of vowel positions that should exchange values while automatically skipping consonants, digits, and punctuation.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n), because each pointer scans across the string at most once.
- Space Complexity: O(n), because Java strings are immutable and the result is built through a character array.

solutions.name: ASCII Lookup Table Two Pointers
solutions.description:
## Approach

Build a constant-size boolean table for printable ASCII vowels, then run the same outside-in two-pointer swap using table lookup instead of repeated string searches.

## Key Insight

The prompt limits input to printable ASCII, so vowel membership can be answered in O(1) by indexing a table. This keeps the reversal idea the same while making membership checks explicit and cheap.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n), because the table is constant-size and the scan is linear.
- Space Complexity: O(n), because the character array holds the mutable result; the lookup table is constant-size.

solutions.name: Collect Vowels Then Refill
solutions.description:
## Approach

First scan the string and collect every vowel character in encounter order. Then scan the character array again; whenever a vowel position appears, fill it with the next collected vowel from the end.

## Key Insight

This separates the task into two simple parts: discover the sequence of vowels, then write that sequence back in reverse while leaving every non-vowel character untouched.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n), because the string is scanned twice.
- Space Complexity: O(n), because the mutable character array and collected vowels may both grow with the input size.

solutions.name: Vowel Index List Swap
solutions.description:
## Approach

Collect the indices of all vowels. Then use two pointers over that index list and swap the characters stored at the paired indices in the character array.

## Key Insight

The vowel positions form the only subsequence that changes. Reversing the characters at those stored positions is equivalent to reversing the vowel subsequence while preserving all other indices.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n), because each character is checked once and each vowel index is swapped at most once.
- Space Complexity: O(n), because the index list can contain every position when the string is all vowels.

solutions.name: Recursive Outside-In Scan
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use a recursive helper on the mutable character array. If the left side is not a vowel, recurse with `left + 1`; if the right side is not a vowel, recurse with `right - 1`; otherwise swap the two vowels and recurse inward.

## Key Insight

This is the same invariant as the iterative two-pointer solution: before each recursive step, everything outside the current range has already been placed correctly. It is useful for teaching the recurrence, though the loop version avoids stack growth.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n), because each recursive step moves at least one boundary inward.
- Space Complexity: O(n), because recursion can use a linear call stack in addition to the result array.

tests.description: Canonical lowercase word reverses two vowels.
Multiple vowels reverse while consonants stay fixed.
Lowercase and uppercase vowels both participate.
String with no vowels remains unchanged.
Mixed-case vowels reverse across the full string.
All-uppercase vowels reverse as a block.
All-lowercase vowels reverse as a block.
The letter y is not a vowel in this problem.
Digits and punctuation stay at their original indices.
Project-themed word checks uppercase and lowercase vowels with consonants fixed.
Longer word checks five vowels and mixed case preservation.
